Planned: being designed now

Community AI

Every civic tool here gets smarter with AI. The plan is to make that intelligence belong to the community too: openly licensed models, running on machines the town owns, over the fiber Longmont already built.

See how Longmont could startRead the essay
Ownthe core

Community machines run the public service and the civic apps, and hold the city's sensitive work.

Rentthe overflow

When demand spikes, the gateway sends routine work to whichever host serves the same open models best that week.

Keepthe switch

Open models and a standard API mean no single company can raise the price or change the terms on you.

From one computer to a whole region

Local AI already works on one machine. The utility takes it to the town, and linked utilities take it to the region.

Why a town can pull this off

Five things are already true.

  • Sharing multiplies the machine.A machine can serve many people at once for barely more effort than one. LMSYS measured a small model on a single desktop AI machine going from 20.5 tokens per second for one user to 368 for 32 requests, about 18 times the output from the same box. LMSYS
  • Civic questions share their homework.When many residents ask about the same public records, the shared part is worked out once and reused. The SGLang research reported up to 6.4 times the throughput on that kind of workload. SGLang paper
  • Open models are right behind.Epoch AI found the best open models have trailed the best closed ones by about four months on average in 2026. That's plenty for summarizing a meeting, searching records or drafting a grant letter. Epoch AI
  • The fiber is in the ground.NextLight already connects the town. In 2026 PCMag's readers named it the top internet provider in America. Broadband Breakfast
  • The software exists.Almost every piece is already open source: the serving engines, the gateway, the chat page and the encrypted network. The work is putting them together for a town.

How it fits together

A tap, a meter and rules, a treatment plant, pipes, and separate secure plumbing where it's needed. Here is the whole system on one page.

The five layers

  1. The front door

    A chat page residents sign into with their library card, plus a standard API that any app can point at by changing one web address.

    LibreChat for the page. The OpenAI-style API that nearly every open tool already speaks.

  2. The gateway

    Where the cooperative's rules become code: a key for every member and app, a meter on every request, fair monthly allowances, routing, and automatic fallback when a machine is down.

    LiteLLM already does keys, budgets and routing.

  3. The serving engines

    Software that batches many people's requests through one machine at once, plus specialty models for meeting transcription and records search.

    vLLM and SGLang on the core. llama.cpp on member desktops.

  4. The hardware

    Three pools: a core the community owns, a locked-down protected pool for city records, and spare capacity members lend.

    A few 128 GB-class machines to start. Grow with measured demand.

  5. The network

    NextLight fiber underneath, with an encrypted private network on top. Member machines only ever call out, so nobody reaches into a home network.

    WireGuard-style encryption. Outbound-only nodes.

Three pools of computers

The core

Owned by the cooperative or nonprofit, in a real room with real power, cooling and backups. Runs the public service and the civic apps. Starts with a few machines, not a rack.

The protected pool

Separate, locked-down hardware for city records. Its own network, its own accounts, full audit logs, and nothing leaves the building.

The member pool

Spare capacity lent by residents, businesses and the makerspace for patient public work, like overnight transcription of a backlog of meeting video.

Answers with the receipts

When a resident asks when the city first considered a development proposal, the answer shouldn't come from a model's memory. The system searches an index of the real public records, hands the right passages to the model, and the model writes an answer that cites them.

The records do the remembering. The model does the reading and writing. It's cheaper, more accurate and easy to check.

Neighbors lending spare machines

A member installs a small program, picks which models to host and when, and the machine asks the cooperative for whole jobs, one machine start to finish. Only public, low-sensitivity work ever goes to a member's computer.

The cooperative checks the work with compact fingerprints of each job, a method called TOPLOC that catches swapped models without rerunning anything, and pays credits under a published formula. TOPLOC

Then towns link up

An illustration of the plan. No other town has signed on yet.

Once one community has a working service, joining others mostly means agreeing on a few standards: the same API, a shared catalog of models, data-sensitivity tags that travel with every request, and plain settlement between cooperatives, the way libraries handle interlibrary loans.

If one cooperative stumbles, the others keep running. Every improvement is shared.

Paid for by the people who use it

Member dues tiered for residents, nonprofits and businesses. Metered use above an included allowance. Contracts with the city, the library and the schools. Grants for a public allocation, so people without money or hardware still get access.

And every quarter, the cooperative publishes what it costs and what it delivered.

How Longmont could start

Ten steps, each one useful on its own.

  1. Form the organization and its rules: membership, pricing, data classes, privacy and retention.
  2. Stand up the core: a handful of machines on the fiber, a small and a mid-size model, speech-to-text and records search, behind the gateway.
  3. Connect the civic apps. TownReporter, CivicCast Brief, TownRecord and TownLight become the first users on day one.
  4. Build the public records index, so residents get answers linked to the source documents.
  5. Open the public door, starting with library card holders.
  6. Build the protected environment for approved city work, with its own hardware, network and audit trail.
  7. Add member machines, starting with makerspace and business computers for overnight batch work.
  8. Wire in rented overflow for low-sensitivity work, from competing hosts serving the same open models.
  9. Measure and publish cost, quality, uptime and use.
  10. Package it so the next town can run the same system, and start linking up with the neighbors.

Share the computing. Keep the public's data public.

Longmont already proved it can own world-class digital infrastructure. The fiber is in the ground, and almost all of the software exists. When it works, give it away.
